rows.w: A Michelin Plate stall and Chomp Chomp's most famous name — thick yellow noodles and bee hoon fried with prawns and squid in a prawn stock simmered for hours, finished with a dollop of sambal. The go-to plate at Serangoon Gardens' legendary supper hawker centre.

rows.n: Hougang Oyster Omelette & Fried Kway Teow
rows.w: A 30-year Hougang heritage stall run by Mr and Mrs Ong that still fries its oyster omelette in pork lard, with big juicy oysters and a fragrant char kway teow alongside. One of the island's best-rated orh luak, worth the queue.

Third- and fourth-generation hawkers who have fried their wet-style Hokkien mee to the same recipe since 1960 — whole prawns, squid rings and pork belly over noodles and bee hoon fried dry so they drink up a prawn-head-and-pork-rib stock, with free-flow crispy lard. Named for its old Simon Road home, now relocated to Kovan 209.

Widely cited as Singapore's best-rated fish soup — a clean, refined broth from a couple who started at Zion Road Blk 91 in 2002 before landing under a quiet Hougang coffeeshop. The 'hei bai' bowl of fried and sliced fish together, done with milk, is the order.

A Hougang corner-stall congee institution with a perpetual 30-minute queue — thick, hearty bowls of smooth Cantonese-style porridge piled with generous ingredients, warming Hougang residents for decades.

The standout orh luak of Chomp Chomp — eggs and starch fried until charred and crisp at the edges around plump, briny oysters, drizzled with tangy chilli. A perennial pick across the centre's food-guide round-ups.

Chicken wings are practically Chomp Chomp's mascot, and Good Luck (Stall 29) grills some of the most sought-after — burnished, charred-edged skin over juicy meat, at roughly S$1.30 a wing. A supper staple of the Serangoon Gardens crowd.

Chomp Chomp's best sambal BBQ seafood — fresh, flaky stingray blanketed in an addictive sambal and grilled on a banana leaf (from S$12 for a small), plus BBQ sotong and cockles. A late-night favourite that draws its own queue.

rows.n: Ang Sar Lee Satay Bee Hoon
rows.w: A 40-plus-year Chomp Chomp veteran plating thin bee hoon drowned in a fragrant satay peanut gravy with cuttlefish, prawns, pork and tau pok — the Serangoon Gardens rendition of a dish few hawkers still make well.
The lunch-hour queue of Kovan 209 — a heaped plate of Hainanese-style chye png flooded with curry, braise and pork gravies, with fried pork chop and cabbage. Old-school comfort food.

A Serangoon Gardens institution since 1983 — the Hainanese founders opened a chicken rice stall, then hired a Nonya chef, and today it is rated among Singapore's best traditional Hainanese chicken rice with a Peranakan zi char spread.

rows.n: Seng Kee Mushroom Minced Meat Noodle
rows.w: A 40-plus-year mushroom minced-meat noodle stall — dry mee pok balanced with a house chilli, deep slow-braised mushroom sauce and crispy pork lard, plus a fish-maw soup its regulars swear by. One of Serangoon Garden Market's most cited names.

One of Singapore's best Teochew braised duck rice stalls, tucked in Hougang's Hainanese Village Centre (Lorong Ah Soo). Tender lean duck over yam rice, drenched in a mildly sweet-savoury five-spice sauce, with an anchovy-loaded sambal. Opens at dawn and usually sells out by early lunch.

rows.n: Hougang Tou Mu Kung (Kew Ong Yah Temple)
rows.w: Singapore's oldest temple dedicated to the Nine Emperor Gods (Kew Ong Yah), completed 1921 and gazetted a National Monument on 14 Jan 2005. Its blend of Hokkien and later Teochew roof forms anchors Hougang's Teochew heritage, and it remains the focus of the annual Nine Emperor Gods Festival.

rows.w: Singapore's last surviving mainland village, established in 1956 when traditional-medicine seller Sng Teow Koon bought the swampy land and rented plots to Malay and Chinese families. A cluster of zinc-roofed houses on dirt tracks around a surau, in the Trafalgar (Buangkok) subzone of Hougang; Ms Sng Mui Hong, the founder's youngest daughter, still lives here as landlord. Old four-digit street signs survive.

rows.w: One of two Chomp Chomp stalls listed in the MICHELIN Guide with a Michelin Plate — skewers grilled over charcoal to order, a supper-time institution best eaten late at Serangoon Gardens with a plate of BBQ chicken wings alongside.

The most-recommended stall in the market — a Muslim-owned nasi lemak (from S$3) built on freshly squeezed coconut milk, pandan-scented rice and a shiok sambal, with crisp ikan bilis and add-ons. Serangoon Gardens' daytime counterpoint to Chomp Chomp.

rows.n: Church of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary
rows.w: A National Monument (gazetted 14 Jan 2005) and the historic heart of Serangoon's Teochew Catholic community, which was mostly farmers in the 19th century. The present Gothic church — pointed arches, a soaring nave — was blessed on 8 Dec 1901 and restored in 2019; the mission dates to pioneer priest Fr Ambrose Maistre in 1852.

rows.w: Serangoon Gardens' legendary supper hawker centre, open since 1972 with around 36 stalls. A night-time institution for BBQ stingray and sotong, Hokkien mee, satay, satay bee hoon, orh luak and charcoal chicken wings — as much a neighbourhood landmark as an eating spot.

A MICHELIN Guide-listed stall that pairs fragrant coconut rice with Ayam Taliwang, the fiery Lombok-style grilled chicken — the smoky, chilli-slicked bird against the cool creamy rice. The Ci Yuan branch of a beloved north-east name, right in Hougang.

A 40-year neighbourhood bakery baking from 2am — classic coconut, cream-puff, chicken-sausage and curry buns from S$1.10, all made from scratch. A generational fixture inside the market.

A 30-year hawker Western stall at Hainanese Village Centre — crispy-outside, tender-inside chicken cutlet, chicken chop, pork chop and fish & chips. Old-school flame-grilled plates at hawker prices.
A Korean-owned hawker stall at Ci Yuan turning out legit Korean fried chicken — crackly-crisp, in flavours like honey butter — from around S$6.50. Hawker-priced KFC done properly.

A corner-kopitiam stall two minutes from Kovan MRT doing all-day Western breakfasts — big brekkies, pancakes, creamy scrambled eggs — at hawker prices from S$3.90. Cafe brunch without the cafe markup.

One of Singapore's oldest private landed estates, laid out in the 1950s by British developer Steven Charles Macey to house British, Australian and NZ servicemen from the nearby RAF Chia Keng camp — which is why nearly every street bears a British name. The Circus roundabout is its social heart, ringed by Chomp Chomp, the market and myVillage.

A tonkatsu specialist at myVillage by Chef Tan, using Sangenton pork air-flown from Japan, each loin tenderised and breaded only on order for a super-crunchy cutlet. Serangoon Gardens' go-to for premium katsu and ramen.

rows.n: Tian Wai Tian Fish Head Steamboat
rows.w: A tiny, wildly popular Kovan streetside zi char serving Teochew-style fish head steamboat in traditional charcoal aluminium pots — pomfret, red grouper or bighead carp — plus salted-egg pork ribs and prawn-paste chicken. Usually packed out by 5.30pm.
A family-run Kovan zi char eatery famed for its fragrant curry fish head, otah and the home-style dishes the family fancies — a low-key neighbourhood favourite off Hougang Street 21.
A roadside Upper Serangoon stall within walking distance of Kovan MRT, packed each morning for handmade Teochew kueh — soon kueh, png kueh — bursting with well-seasoned fillings and made fresh daily.

Billed as Singapore's first heartland izakaya — a 'standing bar' under an HDB block in Kovan serving good Japanese street food late into the night (till 2am on Saturdays). A neighbourhood spot for a late plate and a drink.

A Kovan 209 Hokkien mee stall run by the former cook of Teow Heng Cooked Food. A big plate of thick and thin noodles with prawns, cuttlefish and pork lard in a seafood broth, fried with wok hei to spare — the 'Davis Prawn Noodles' are the house signature.

A hidden gem at Hainanese Village Centre serving just two dishes — fried Hokkien prawn mee and char kway teow — with almost everything made from scratch: the prawn stock, pork lard, chilli, even hand-peeled garlic. Run by Mrs Lu and her husband for over a decade.

rows.n: Lorong Ah Soo Lor Mee (Fu Yuan Mei Shi)
rows.w: A long-loved Hainanese Village Centre stall drawing crowds for its lor mee — flat noodles under a luscious thick gravy with a secret ingredient — and laksa. A Hougang breakfast-crowd fixture.

A humble 50-year wanton mee tucked in a back corner of Chomp Chomp (no relation to the bakery of the same name) — springy noodles, silky-skinned wantons and char siew all made in-house, in a broth with robust ikan-bilis notes.

The other half of Chomp Chomp's Hokkien mee debate — a darker, wetter plate with its own loyal supporters who rate it over Ah Hock. Between the two, Serangoon Gardens arguably has Singapore's densest Hokkien mee rivalry.

rows.n: Lao Song Fa (Botanical Garden Famous Fishball Noodle)
rows.w: An old-name fishball noodle stall carrying the 'Botanical Garden Famous' lineage — springy mee pok tossed with handmade fishballs, fishcake and minced pork, a market staple for decades.
A market prawn-noodle mainstay, its rich prawn-and-pork broth a recurring recommendation in the Serangoon Garden Market guides.
A three-in-one stall doing moist, well-coated Hokkien mee in a velvety prawn stock (about S$3.50), plus fried oyster and white/black carrot cake with eggy bits and preserved radish.

rows: 1 place · kept for the record, newest check first

rows.w: A well-loved Kovan brunch cafe for specialty coffee and toasted jaffles in a light, plant-filled space — it closed on 19 Jan 2025. Kept here as a flagged closure.
